methodology.note: Les conclusions concernent les usages alimentaires documentes. Une origine naturelle, une ADI non numerique ou une autorisation ne constitue pas une garantie d'absence de risque; les usages de complements a forte dose ne sont pas transferes automatiquement aux additifs alimentaires.

additives.chemicalFamily: Betalains; beetroot red preparation with betanin as principal colouring compound

regulatoryStatus.conditions: EU specifications and authorised use conditions apply; nitrate content must be controlled for the additive preparation.

adi.status: JECFA: not specified under good manufacturing practice

adiHistory.type: ADI not specified; nitrate specification condition

healthEffects.finding: JECFA's relevant condition concerns control of nitrate as a component of beetroot red; this is a specification issue and not evidence of a general toxic effect of betanin at authorised food use.
healthEffects.population: general population; particular attention to foods for infants and young children

sensitivePopulations: Infants and young children, for whom nitrate content in foods requires particular control.

exposureAssessment.officialConclusion: JECFA considered beetroot red usable according to good manufacturing practice with an ADI not specified, provided nitrate levels meet specifications.
exposureAssessment.productSpecificConclusion: The preparation composition, nitrate level and amount in the scanned product are unknown.

additives.scientificSummary: E162 is a preparation whose principal pigment is betanin, not an isolated single molecule in every commercial preparation. JECFA assigned an ADI not specified under good manufacturing practice, with a specific nitrate-content condition. This supports no particular signal for the authorised food use, without treating natural origin as an absolute safety guarantee.

sources.title: Food colours: E162 safety assessment status

limitations: The additive preparation and nitrate level are not available in the product data.
The OpenFoodTox record has no numeric reference value.

regulatoryStatus.conditions: EU specifications and conditions of use apply; purity and contaminant specifications remain relevant.

adi.status: No numerical ADI considered necessary by EFSA; JECFA: not limited for calcium carbonate, conditional on acceptable calcium dietary load

adiHistory.type: ADI not limited; calcium dietary load to be considered
EFSA re-evaluation; no numerical ADI needed
follow-up for specifications and infant uses

healthEffects.finding: EFSA reported no safety concern for calcium carbonate per se at reported food-additive uses and levels, while noting that calcium contribution is only a small part of overall exposure in the assessed context.
healthEffects.population: general population and infants in the assessed food categories

healthEffects.finding: EFSA identified the need to address unavoidable aluminium and other contaminant specifications; this is a quality/specification data gap, not an automatic conclusion that ordinary E170 use is hazardous.
healthEffects.population: all consumers; dependent on additive purity

sensitivePopulations: People with high total calcium intake or relevant medical conditions; this cannot be inferred from the presence of E170 alone.

exposureAssessment.officialConclusion: JECFA placed no restriction on calcium carbonate when dietary calcium load is acceptable. EFSA found no need for a numerical ADI for E170 per se in assessed uses, while requesting follow-up data on specifications and contaminants.
exposureAssessment.productSpecificConclusion: The quantity of E170, total calcium intake and impurity profile of the scanned product are unknown.

additives.scientificSummary: Official assessments do not identify a particular signal for calcium carbonate at authorised food-additive uses. The calcium contribution, purity specifications and contaminant data remain relevant limitations; high-dose calcium supplementation must not be attributed automatically to E170 in food.

sources.title: Re-evaluation of calcium carbonate (E 170) as a food additive
Call for technical and toxicological data on calcium carbonate (E 170)

limitations: The scanned product's calcium amount and additive purity are unknown.
The conclusion does not assess high-dose calcium supplementation.

additives.chemicalFamily: Sorbates; group evaluation with E202 and E203

regulatoryStatus.conditions: Authorised uses and maximum levels are defined by the EU additive framework.

adi.appliesTo: sorbic acid (E200), potassium sorbate (E202) and calcium sorbate (E203) as applicable to the group assessment

adiHistory.type: temporary group value discussed during follow-up

healthEffects.finding: EFSA found no evidence of genotoxic activity for the sorbate group in the re-evaluation used here.

exposureAssessment.officialConclusion: EFSA's follow-up exposure estimates were below the current group ADI at mean and high exposure levels for the assessed population groups.
exposureAssessment.productSpecificConclusion: The product concentration and individual total dietary exposure are unknown.

additives.scientificSummary: E200 and E202 belong to the same sorbate group evaluation. The classification is intentionally aligned with the validated E202 record: current group ADI 11 mg sorbic acid/kg bw/day, no genotoxicity signal identified in the cited EFSA assessment, and population exposure estimates below the ADI.

sources.title: Re-evaluation of sorbic acid (E 200), potassium sorbate (E 202) and calcium sorbate (E 203)
Follow-up of the re-evaluation of sorbic acid and potassium sorbate

limitations: The ADI is group-based and expressed as sorbic acid.

additives.chemicalFamily: Lactic acid; stereoisomers and food-grade preparation

regulatoryStatus.conditions: EU rules permit lactic acid as a food additive under the applicable conditions, including quantum satis contexts.

adi.status: JECFA: not limited in the historical food-additive evaluation

healthEffects.finding: Lactic acid is a normal metabolic intermediate and food acidulant; the official food-additive conclusion does not identify a major systemic toxicological signal at intended food use. Local acidity depends on the food matrix and amount consumed.
healthEffects.population: general population; matrix and exposure dependent

exposureAssessment.officialConclusion: JECFA's historical table lists lactic acid as not limited for food-additive use; EFSA describes E270 as a permitted additive and has requested updated use-level data.
exposureAssessment.productSpecificConclusion: The concentration, matrix and individual exposure are unknown.

additives.scientificSummary: The available official material supports no particular signal for E270 in its intended food-additive use. This does not mean zero risk in every context: local acidity and excessive intake depend on the product matrix and exposure, and are not evidence of general systemic toxicity.

sources.title: Food additive evaluation table including lactic acid
Open call for analytical data and use levels: lactic acid (E270)

limitations: The conclusion does not assess pharmacological or supplemental dosing.

regulatoryStatus.conditions: EU additive conditions and specifications apply; E300 is also a naturally occurring nutrient.

adi.status: JECFA: not specified for ascorbic acid and sodium, potassium and calcium ascorbates
adi.appliesTo: ascorbic acid and listed ascorbate salts

adiHistory.unit: mg/kg bw/day additional to natural food intake

healthEffects.finding: Potential gastrointestinal or other effects at high supplemental intakes are not used as an automatic hazard classification for E300 used as an antioxidant in food.
healthEffects.population: consumers of high-dose supplements; not product-specific

exposureAssessment.officialConclusion: JECFA assigned an ADI not specified for the group and recognised the nutrient's normal dietary presence; this applies within good manufacturing practice and intended food use.
exposureAssessment.productSpecificConclusion: The amount of E300 and total vitamin C intake are unknown.

additives.scientificSummary: E300 is vitamin C used as an antioxidant. JECFA's group ADI is not specified, and the historical record includes conditional values before that conclusion. High-dose supplement effects are not transferred automatically to food-additive use.

sources.title: Food additives and naturally occurring substances

limitations: The product quantity and total vitamin C intake are unavailable.
High-dose supplement effects are outside the product-specific assessment.

additives.chemicalFamily: Mixture rich in tocopherols; composition depends on source and preparation

regulatoryStatus.conditions: EU specifications and use conditions apply; the exact tocopherol profile and impurities of the preparation are material to the assessment.

adi.status: No ADI established by EFSA; overall toxicology database considered insufficient and additional data requested

adiHistory.type: ADI not established; data gaps identified
follow-up data call for composition, impurities and toxicology

healthEffects.finding: EFSA considered the overall toxicity database insufficient to establish an ADI and requested composition, contaminant, reproductive/developmental and infant-use data.
healthEffects.population: all population groups; specific data requirements for infants below 16 weeks

sensitivePopulations: Infants below 16 weeks, for whom EFSA requested a dedicated risk assessment and additional data.

exposureAssessment.officialConclusion: A definitive safety conclusion and numerical ADI were not established because of identified data gaps; no product-specific exposure can be estimated.
exposureAssessment.productSpecificConclusion: The exact composition, tocopherol ratios, impurities, amount and product exposure are unknown.

additives.scientificSummary: E306 remains insufficient_data. EFSA explicitly identified an insufficient toxicological database for establishing an ADI and requested further composition and toxicology data. No CAS number is present in the OpenFoodTox record, and none is invented here.

sources.title: Re-evaluation of tocopherol-rich extract (E 306), alpha-tocopherol (E 307), gamma-tocopherol (E 308) and delta-tocopherol (E 309)
Call for technical and toxicological data on tocopherol-rich extract and tocopherols

limitations: The EFSA data gaps prevent a positive safety classification.
E306 is a mixture and the OpenFoodTox record has no CAS number.
No classification beyond insufficient_data is inferred from the absence of an ADI.

additives.chemicalFamily: Mixture of phospholipids/phosphatides, including phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylinositol

regulatoryStatus.conditions: EU specifications and authorised uses apply; source, purity and residual protein levels are relevant.

adi.status: JECFA: not limited based on biochemical and nutritional experience

healthEffects.finding: EFSA identified case reports of hypersensitivity associated with soy and egg lecithins and requested information on residual proteins. This is a source- and preparation-dependent allergenicity issue, not evidence that lecithins are a general toxic hazard.
healthEffects.population: people sensitised to relevant soy or egg proteins

sensitivePopulations: People with soy or egg allergy, depending on the lecithin source and residual protein content.

exposureAssessment.officialConclusion: JECFA set an ADI not limited for lecithin, while EFSA identified residual-protein and infant-use data gaps requiring follow-up.
exposureAssessment.productSpecificConclusion: The source (soy, egg or another permitted source), residual proteins, amount and product exposure are unknown.

additives.scientificSummary: E322 is not classified as a general danger because it may originate from soy or egg. The relevant signal is targeted hypersensitivity related to residual proteins and source, while JECFA's toxicological assessment supports an ADI not limited for lecithin meeting specifications.

sources.title: Re-evaluation of lecithins (E 322) as a food additive
Call for technical and toxicological data on lecithins (E 322)

limitations: The product does not identify the lecithin source or residual protein level.
The allergy signal is individual and source-dependent.
The conclusion does not classify soy or egg allergy risk for an unlabelled product.
